opus-5.5.text:
I think that's an overstatement, or at least it's a story that's a bit neater than what actually happened.

There's certainly equivariance in AlphaFold 2. The structure module, with invariant point attention, is built so that if you rotate or translate the whole protein, the outputs transform the way they should. That's a nice property, and I'm happy we have it. But if you look at where most of the computation happens, it's in the Evoformer, and the Evoformer isn't equivariant in any geometric sense. It works on the pair representation and the MSA representation, which are essentially about relationships between residues, not coordinates in 3D space. A huge amount of the "figuring out the structure" happens there before you ever touch 3D coordinates.

When we ran ablations, removing or weakening the equivariant parts hurt, but not catastrophically. It wasn't the single thing holding the whole system up. What mattered more was a whole collection of ideas working together: the representations we chose, letting the network reason about the pair representation with triangle-style updates, recycling, end-to-end training through the structure, the right losses, the self-distillation. No single one of those is "the" answer. You get a few points here, a few points there, and they compound.

So I'd frame equivariance less as a victory and more as one good engineering decision among many. It's a useful inductive bias, and in places where it's cheap and natural, you should use it. But I'd caution people against concluding that if you just make everything equivariant you'll solve your problem. In our experience the bigger wins came from thinking carefully about how information should flow through the network and what the network should be able to reason about, and then letting the data do a lot of the work.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back on it a bit, honestly. I understand why people say it, because the structure module in AlphaFold 2 is built around frames and it respects rotations and translations in a very explicit way, so it looks like a triumph of geometric deep learning. But if you ask me what actually made the system work, equivariance isn't near the top of the list.

The things that mattered were the way we represented the problem: reasoning jointly over pairs of residues, the triangle updates that let the network enforce something like geometric consistency in the pair representation, iterating between sequence and pair information in the Evoformer, recycling, and training on the right objectives with a lot of care. Those are about getting the network to think about the physics and the evolutionary signal properly. The equivariance in the structure module was a nice, clean way to generate coordinates, and I do think it helped with data efficiency, but I don't think it was the decisive ingredient.

And the evidence since then points the same direction. People have built systems that drop the equivariant machinery and just use coordinates with augmentation, and they work fine, sometimes better. AlphaFold 3 moved toward a diffusion approach that doesn't rely on the same frame-based construction. So I'd say equivariance was a useful engineering choice in a particular place, not the reason the problem got solved. The real lesson of AlphaFold 2, for me, is that you win by taking the structure of the problem seriously, and there are many ways to do that.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s partly right, but it depends on what you mean by equivariance. If you mean that respecting the geometry of the problem was important, then absolutely. But if you mean that AlphaFold 2 succeeded because we made the whole network equivariant, that’s not really the story.

A lot of the computation happens in the Evoformer, where we’re reasoning about sequences and relationships between residues, without an explicit three-dimensional structure. Then the structure module uses invariant point attention to bring geometry into the calculation. That lets it reason about spatial relationships without depending on an arbitrary choice of coordinates.

So equivariance was a useful ingredient. I’d be cautious about turning that into a claim that it was the decisive ingredient. The challenge was getting evolutionary information, learning, and geometry to work together. You can explain why a particular architectural choice makes sense without having established that it explains the system’s success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s only partly right. Equivariance was an important ingredient, particularly in the structure module, but I wouldn’t describe AlphaFold 2 as primarily a victory for equivariance. A lot of the computation happens in representations that don’t have explicit three-dimensional coordinates at all: the multiple sequence alignment and the pair representation.

The question was really where to put the geometric constraints. You want the answer to behave sensibly if you rotate or translate the protein, but that doesn’t mean every part of the network needs to be an equivariant network. We used geometry where it helped, while giving the rest of the system room to learn. So I’d be cautious about taking the success of the whole system as proof that any one architectural principle was the decisive ingredient.
